title: Consistent Hashing for a Distributed KV Cluster
problem: Design a distributed KV cluster that spreads keys across N shards, routes requests to the owning shard in O(1), replicates for durability, and rebalances with minimal key movement when nodes are added or removed.
summary: A coordinator-fronted KV cluster built on a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes (vnodes) — the technique. The chapter's canonical hash function is SHA-1 over a 2^160 ring (real systems like Dynamo/Cassandra use MD5, MurmurHash, or similar truncated to 128 or 32 bits — the ring shape is identical). Each physical shard is mapped onto the ring at multiple vnode positions so ownership is uniformly distributed even with small cluster sizes; the book cites an experiment showing std-dev drops to ~10% at 100 vnodes and ~5% at 200. Keys are hashed into the ring, and each key is owned by the first shard clockwise (plus N-1 more for replication). When a shard joins or leaves, only keys on the arc between it and its predecessor move — k/n keys on average per Karger et al., not ~k as with modulo hashing. The chapter's wrap-up calls out consistent hashing as the technique used in Dynamo, Cassandra, Discord, Akamai CDN, and Google's Maglev load balancer. Dominant tradeoff: vnode count — too few and load skews; too many and ring maintenance + gossip state grows linearly.

functional: addNode(nodeId) places a physical node on the ring using V virtual node positions
removeNode(nodeId) atomically removes all V vnodes belonging to that node
getNode(key) returns the owning physical node in O(log V*N) via binary search on a sorted ring
getReplicas(key, n) returns the next N distinct physical nodes clockwise for replication
Ring membership is observable (size, node list, vnode positions) for rebalance tooling
Node joins/leaves report the exact set of keys that need to migrate to/from each peer
nonFunctional: Lookup latency sub-microsecond for rings up to ~10,000 vnodes
Standard deviation of per-node load under 10% with >=100 vnodes per physical node
Membership changes move only K/N keys on average, never more than 2*K/N in the worst case
Ring state is small (~50 KB for 600 vnodes) so it propagates via gossip in seconds
Thread-safe reads concurrent with rare writes (node add/remove) using copy-on-write or read-write locks
Deterministic placement: same (nodeId, vnodeIndex) always hashes to the same ring position across processes

assumptions: 4 physical shards, replication factor N=3, W=2 acks on write (Dynamo-style quorum extension; the book itself does not discuss N/W/R but the ring is the same)
150 virtual nodes per physical shard (600 vnodes on the ring) — in the band the book's referenced experiment identifies as giving ~5-10% std dev of load
Hash space: chapter's canonical example is SHA-1 (2^160); this design uses MurmurHash3 truncated to 2^32 for cheaper lookup. Shape is identical either way.
Expected dataset ~1B keys at ~1 KB each (~1 TB total, ~750 GB per shard with RF=3)
estimates: Per-shard ownership with 150 vnodes: std-dev of load ~5-10% (chapter reference [2] experiment: 100 vnodes → 10%, 200 vnodes → 5%)
Adding a 5th shard rebalances ~1/5 of the keyspace ≈ 200 GB of data movement (vs ~100% with naive modulo hashing — the chapter's 'cache miss storm' scenario)
Rebalance throughput budget ≈ 100 MB/s per shard → ~35 min to drain a neighbour's share
Coordinator routing cost: 1 hash + 1 binary search on sorted ring (~600 entries) ≈ sub-microsecond
Gossip/membership state: 600 vnodes * ~80 B/entry ≈ 50 KB per node — trivial to replicate via gossip

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client] --> coord[Coordinator] coord --> ring[Consistent-Hash Ring] ring --> s1[(Shard A)] ring --> s2[(Shard B)] ring --> s3[(Shard C)] ring --> s4[(Shard D)] rebal[Rebalancer] --> ring rebal --> s1 rebal --> s2 rebal --> s3 rebal --> s4

client.name: Client SDK
client.summary: Thin client library that sends PUT/GET to a coordinator and retries on transient failures.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Send `PUT key value` and `GET key` over gRPC/HTTP to any coordinator
- Attach an idempotency id on writes for safe retry
- On 503 (quorum not met) or timeout, retry with small exponential backoff

sections.heading: Client-side hashing (optional)
sections.body: Smart clients embed the ring and hash locally, then hit the owner shard directly — skipping the coordinator hop. Worth it at >10K QPS per client; adds complexity around ring refresh.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: The client only needs to know ONE coordinator address. The hash ring is a server-side abstraction — the client never computes which shard owns a key.

lost: Client must keep ring in sync via gossip
Schema/routing changes must roll through all clients

bottlenecks.title: Coordinator hotspot from dumb-client fan-in
bottlenecks.trigger: At peak 50K ops/sec with all clients routing through coordinators (thin-client mode), a single coordinator instance capped at concurrency 5000 and 2-6ms service time can saturate if load balancing is uneven or a coordinator pod is slow
bottlenecks.symptom: Elevated p99 PUT/GET latency (>50ms vs expected 8-20ms), 503 responses, client retry storms amplifying the problem
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable smart-client mode for high-QPS callers (>10K QPS per client) per the design's alternative — embed the ring locally via gossip subscription, skip the coordinator hop, drop service time from [2,8]ms to [1,4]ms
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on coordinator CPU >70% or per-coordinator QPS skew >20% from mean; track client-side retry rate with threshold >1% over 5min

bottlenecks.title: Retry amplification without bounded backoff
bottlenecks.trigger: Client failureRate of 0.0005 plus coordinator 0.0005 means ~0.1% of requests retry; during a coordinator failover or rebalance (35min window), transient 503s spike and naive exponential backoff across 50K ops/sec can add thousands of in-flight retries
bottlenecks.symptom: Thundering herd after any brief coordinator blip; duplicate writes if idempotency_key is missing or mis-scoped; client-visible latency cliff
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce jittered exponential backoff (e.g., AWS full-jitter: sleep = random(0, min(cap, base*2^attempt))), cap retries at 3, and require idempotency_key on every PUT (already in SDK — make it non-optional)
bottlenecks.detection: Track client-side retry_count histogram and duplicate idempotency_key hit-rate at coordinator; alert when retry rate exceeds 2x baseline for >1min

bottlenecks.title: Stale ring cache in smart-client mode during rebalance
bottlenecks.trigger: When shard E joins and rebalance runs ~35min, smart clients with embedded rings at 10s refresh interval will route to the old owner for up to 10s after ring version 18 publishes; during the transfer window, routing can land on a shard that no longer owns the key
bottlenecks.symptom: Intermittent 'key not found' on GET immediately after rebalance commit, or writes landing on the wrong preference list causing read-after-write inconsistency
bottlenecks.mitigation: Subscribe smart clients to gossip membership events for push-based invalidation instead of 10s polling; on receiving a NotOwner error from a shard, force-refresh the ring and retry once against the returned hint
bottlenecks.detection: Emit a NotOwner error metric from storage nodes; alert when NotOwner rate >0.01% of requests or when client ring_version lag behind authoritative ring exceeds 30s

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Client SDK is here In this KV cluster, a key's owner is determined by hashing it onto a ring of 600 vnodes spread across 4 shards. Your application code shouldn't know *any* of that — it just wants `put("user:42", value)` to work. The SDK is the thin shim that hides the ring, the preference list, the W=2 quorum, and the retry logic behind two method calls. Without it, every team using the cluster would re-implement hashing, coordinator discovery, and idempotent retries — and get at least one of them wrong. ## What happens without it Imagine the app talks raw HTTP to a coordinator. A coordinator pod restarts mid-write; the app sees a timeout and naively retries against a different coordinator. No idempotency key means the write lands twice, possibly with different version clocks on different replicas, and now reads return conflicting values that the coordinator has to reconcile. The user sees occasional "ghost" duplicate records; the operator sees conflict-resolution metrics climbing; the storage shards take the hit doing extra work during read repair. ## The number that justifies it Peak load is **50K ops/sec** with a client failure rate of 0.0005 — that's ~25 failed requests/sec that need retrying. At 0.1% retry volume across 50K ops/sec, naive retries without jittered backoff and idempotency keys would amplify into thousands of duplicate in-flight writes during any coordinator blip. Centralizing that logic in the SDK is the only sane place to enforce it once. ## Trade-off You now ship and version a library — every language binding is ongoing maintenance, and old SDK versions lingering in production can mask server-side improvements.

coord.name: Coordinator
coord.summary: Stateless request router: hashes the key, looks up the owning shards on the ring, fans out the request to replicas.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
1. Hash the key (MurmurHash3 → 32-bit token)
2. Look up the preference list (N shards clockwise from the token) on the ring
3. Forward the request to replicas and collect W acks for writes / R reads
4. Return aggregated response to the client

sections.heading: Ring cache
sections.body: The coordinator keeps a local copy of the ring (sorted array of (token, vnode_owner)). It refreshes the ring from the membership layer on gossip events or every 10s.

sections.heading: Stateless + replaceable
sections.body: Coordinators hold no durable state — lose one and another takes over instantly. Typically fronted by an LB or DNS round-robin.

gained: No dedicated coordinator tier — any shard can coordinate
lost: Shards do coordination AND storage → noisy-neighbour risk

bottlenecks.title: Fan-out connection and tail-latency amplification
bottlenecks.trigger: At 50K ops/sec with N=3 replica fan-out per request, the coordinator tier holds ~150K concurrent in-flight replica RPCs. Per-coordinator concurrency cap is 5000; with 2-6ms service time plus waiting for W=2 of 3 acks, any single slow replica (p99 WAL fsync spike on one shard) stretches the coordinator's holding time and consumes the concurrency budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Coordinator p99 PUT latency balloons from ~15ms to >100ms even though shard-local p50 looks healthy; 'concurrency limit reached' rejections return 503; client retry storms amplify load
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable hedged requests on the 3rd replica after p95 latency (e.g., fire to A if B+C haven't both acked within 10ms), and enforce per-replica request budgets with circuit breakers (gRPC deadline 50ms, outlier ejection after 5 consecutive timeouts) so one slow shard can't pin coordinator slots
bottlenecks.detection: Track coordinator in-flight request gauge vs concurrency cap (5000); alert when >80% sustained for >30s. Emit per-replica ack-latency histogram and alert on p99 skew >3x across shards.

bottlenecks.title: Stale ring cache during rebalance or membership flap
bottlenecks.trigger: Coordinator refreshes ring every 10s on gossip events. During the ~35min rebalance window when shard E joins (ring version 17→18), coordinators running the old ring route PUTs to the pre-join preference list while the rebalancer is already streaming keys to E; any coordinator that misses a gossip event routes to wrong owners for up to 10s.
bottlenecks.symptom: Intermittent NotOwner errors from storage nodes, read-after-write failures (PUT on ring v17 preference list, GET on ring v18 sees different replicas), conflict-resolution metrics spike on storage nodes
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tag every RPC with the coordinator's ring_version; storage nodes reject stale-version writes with a hint pointing to the current owner (NotOwner + hint). Switch ring refresh from 10s polling to push-based gossip subscription so version lag stays <1s.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit NotOwner error rate metric from storage nodes; alert when >0.01% of requests. Track max(authoritative_ring_version - coordinator_ring_version) across fleet; alert when lag >15s.

bottlenecks.title: Uneven coordinator load from LB hashing or hot keys
bottlenecks.trigger: With 50K ops/sec split across coordinator pods via DNS round-robin or LB, skew from sticky client connections or a hot key (e.g., celebrity user:42 receiving 5K QPS) can pin one coordinator at concurrency=5000 while peers sit at 20%. Coordinator is stateless so LB can't re-route mid-request without breaking idempotency semantics.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-coordinator CPU/QPS dashboard shows 3-5x skew; one pod hits 503s while others are idle; p99 degrades for a subset of clients even though fleet-average is healthy
bottlenecks.mitigation: Front with an L7 LB using least-outstanding-requests (Envoy LEAST_REQUEST) instead of round-robin; add a small LRU response cache (1000 entries, 100ms TTL) for hot-key GETs at the coordinator to shed read load without hurting consistency beyond the cache window
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-coordinator QPS skew >20% from fleet mean over 5min; track concurrency-limit rejection rate per pod and alert on any single pod >0.1%.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Coordinator is here The problem asks for O(1) routing to the owning shard plus N=3 replication with quorum writes. Someone has to actually *do* that work: hash the key, look up the preference list on the 600-vnode ring, fan out to 3 storage nodes, and wait for W=2 acks before replying. The Coordinator is a stateless tier whose whole job is to be that "someone." It keeps a local cached copy of the ring (refreshed via gossip) so the lookup is a binary search over ~600 entries — sub-microsecond — and the client never needs to know the cluster topology exists. ## What happens without it If you delete this tier, every client app has to embed the ring, subscribe to gossip, and implement quorum logic itself. When you add shard E and publish ring version 18, any client still running ring v17 routes writes to the wrong replicas — the storage node rejects them with NotOwner, the user sees sporadic write failures, and the operator sees conflict-resolution metrics climb on the storage shards because some writes landed on the pre-join preference list and some on the post-join one. The storage tier absorbs all the pain of client bugs. ## The number At peak **50K ops/sec** with N=3 fan-out, the cluster carries ~150K in-flight replica RPCs. Centralizing that fan-out in a stateless tier (concurrency cap 5000 per pod → ~30 coordinator pods) means you scale coordination independently from storage, and a bad client release can't corrupt replica placement. ## Trade-off You pay one extra network hop (~2–6ms) on every request in exchange for keeping clients dumb and the ring server-authoritative.

ring.name: Consistent-Hash Ring
ring.summary: The chapter's core data structure: a circular hash space (canonically SHA-1 over 2^160, here truncated to 2^32) populated with vnode positions for each physical shard. Owns the placement function used by every read and write.

sections.heading: Hash space and ring (per book)
sections.body: Chapter 5 walks through the ring using SHA-1: hash output range 0..2^160-1, joined end-to-end to form a ring. Servers and keys are hashed onto the same ring. To find a key's server, walk clockwise from the key's position until the first server (or vnode) is found. That's the whole algorithm — no modulo.

sections.heading: The rehashing problem this solves
sections.body: With `serverIndex = hash(key) % N`, removing one server changes N and rehashes ~all keys — the chapter's opening example with 4 servers and 8 keys shows cache-miss storms after a single node leaves. Consistent hashing only remaps the arc between the departed node and its predecessor (Karger et al.: k/n keys on average).

sections.heading: Two basic-approach issues (per book)
sections.body:
The raw Karger ring has two problems the chapter calls out before introducing vnodes:
1. **Uneven partitions** — arcs between servers have wildly different sizes, so one server owns a much larger slice.
2. **Non-uniform key distribution** — even with equal arcs, random hashing can cluster keys onto a subset of servers.
Both are solved by virtual nodes.

sections.heading: Data structure
sections.body: A sorted array of `(token, vnode_id, shard_id)` tuples, one per vnode. Lookup is `upper_bound(hash(key))` — binary search, O(log V) where V = total vnodes (here 600).

sections.heading: Why virtual nodes
sections.body: Without vnodes, 4 shards → 4 points on the ring → uneven arcs → skewed load. Each server gets multiple vnode positions. Chapter reference [2] reports std-dev of ~10% at 100 vnodes and ~5% at 200 vnodes of the mean ownership — we use 150 for a middle-ground. Cost: more vnodes → more ring state to store and gossip, so this is a tunable tradeoff.

sections.heading: Preference list
sections.body: For replication factor N, walk clockwise from the key's token and collect the first N distinct physical owners as the preference list. Distinct-owner filter ensures replicas land on different shards, not different vnodes of the same shard. (The chapter itself doesn't cover replication — this is the Dynamo extension.)

sections.heading: Affected-range math (per book)
sections.body: On add: the affected arc runs anticlockwise from the new server to its predecessor on the ring — only keys in that arc migrate to the new server. On remove: the affected arc runs anticlockwise from the removed server to its predecessor — those keys move to the clockwise successor. This is the chapter's 'Find affected keys' section.

sections.heading: Real-world deployments (per book)
sections.body:
Chapter 5's wrap-up lists notable production uses:
- Partitioning in Amazon Dynamo
- Data partitioning across Apache Cassandra
- Discord chat
- Akamai CDN
- Google's Maglev network load balancer

lost: Adding/removing a shard remaps ~100% of keys — catastrophic for a live cluster
Any cluster size change = full rebalance
Only supports appending shards (no arbitrary add/remove)

gained: No sorted-ring maintenance — compute a weight per shard and pick max
lost: O(S) per lookup vs O(log V) for ring
Higher CPU cost when S is large

bottlenecks.title: Vnode count growth bloats ring state and gossip churn
bottlenecks.trigger: Current 150 vnodes/shard × 4 shards = 600 entries (~50 KB). Scaling to 50 shards at the same 150 vnodes yields 7,500 entries (~600 KB); pushing vnodes to 200 for better balance (5% std-dev per the chapter reference) at 50 shards yields 10,000 entries. Every membership event re-gossips the full delta to all coordinators and storage nodes.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gossip bandwidth spikes and ring-refresh CPU on coordinators climbs during rolling restarts; ring lookup binary search L1-cache-misses on hot paths; ring publish takes seconds instead of sub-second, widening the stale-cache window for coordinators routing on ring v17 while v18 is committing.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap vnodes per shard at 150 (the design's chosen middle-ground) and switch to weighted ring entries when shards have heterogeneous capacity rather than adding more vnodes; ship ring deltas (added/removed token tuples) over gossip instead of full snapshots; store the ring as a single contiguous sorted uint32 token array + parallel uint16 shard_id array for cache-friendly binary search.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ring_size_bytes > 500 KB or gossip_message_size p99 > 100 KB; track ring_publish_latency_ms and alert when > 1s; monitor coordinator ring_refresh_cpu_pct and alert > 5% sustained.

bottlenecks.title: Preference-list walk degenerates with clustered vnodes of same shard
bottlenecks.trigger: The distinct-owner filter walks clockwise until N=3 distinct physical shards are found. With 150 vnodes × 4 shards = 600 entries, random placement produces runs where 5–10 consecutive vnodes belong to the same shard (birthday-paradox clustering). For N=3 on a 4-shard cluster, the walk occasionally scans 20+ entries before finding 3 distinct owners — at 50K ops/sec, every PUT/GET does this walk.
bottlenecks.symptom: Ring lookup p99 drifts from sub-microsecond to 5–10 µs; under load, coordinator CPU shows unexpected time in ring.preference_list; worse on 4-shard clusters (the current size) where distinct-owner scarcity is highest.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Precompute and cache the preference list per vnode token at ring-publish time (600 entries × 3 shard_ids = ~7 KB), turning the per-request walk into a single array lookup. Invalidate on ring version bump.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram ring_lookup_ns at p50/p99/p999; alert when p99 > 2 µs or when preference_list_walk_depth p99 > 10 entries.

bottlenecks.title: Load skew under small cluster size despite 150 vnodes
bottlenecks.trigger: Chapter reference [2] gives ~5–10% std-dev of ownership at 100–200 vnodes/shard assuming uniform hash distribution. With only 4 shards (600 total vnodes), worst-case shard can own 15–20% more than the mean; combined with a hot key or hot range (e.g., sequential timestamp-prefixed keys hashing to a narrow arc), one shard sees disproportionate QPS of the 50K ops/sec budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-shard QPS dashboard shows one shard at 15K ops/sec while others sit at 11K; that shard's WAL fsync p99 spikes first during traffic bursts; coordinator sees uneven replica ack latency skewing the W=2 completion tail.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Bump vnodes to 200/shard when cluster size ≤ 6 (per the chapter's referenced experiment, drops std-dev to ~5%); add key-prefix salting in the SDK for known sequential-key workloads; monitor per-shard ownership_pct and rebalance vnode assignments (not data) when drift > 12% from mean.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit per-shard owned_token_fraction gauge; alert when max/min ratio > 1.25. Track per-shard qps and alert on >20% skew from fleet mean over 5 min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the ring is here The problem asks for two things that fight each other: route every key to its owner shard in near-constant time, *and* rebalance with minimal key movement when shards join or leave. The obvious approach — `shard = hash(key) % N` — nails the first requirement but catastrophically fails the second. The moment N changes from 4 to 5, almost every key's modulo result shifts, so ~100% of the 1 TB dataset has to move. The Consistent-Hash Ring is the data structure that satisfies both requirements simultaneously: keys and shards live on the same circular hash space, and each key is owned by the first shard clockwise from its position. ## What happens without it Swap the ring for modulo hashing and add a 5th shard. Every coordinator starts routing reads to the "new" owner for almost every key — but the data hasn't moved there yet. Users see a cluster-wide cache-miss storm; the operator watches every shard simultaneously saturated with cross-shard backfill traffic; the rebalancer, which expected to move ~200 GB, is now trying to move ~1 TB while live traffic collapses. This is the exact "cache miss storm" scenario Chapter 5 opens with. ## The number Adding a 5th shard moves **~1/5 of the keyspace ≈ 200 GB** instead of ~100% ≈ 1 TB — a 5× reduction. At the rebalancer's 100 MB/s budget, that's ~35 minutes of drain versus ~2.8 hours. The ring turns a half-day outage into a coffee break. ## Trade-off You accept ~50 KB of ring state per node and the complexity of tuning vnode count (150 here) to keep load std-dev around 5–10%.

s1.name: Shard A (Storage Node)
s1.summary: LSM-backed storage node owning ~150 vnodes' worth of the ring (RocksDB under the hood).

sections.heading: Storage engine
sections.body: Embedded RocksDB (or similar LSM). Key → bytes. Writes go to WAL + memtable, flush to SSTs, background compaction.

sections.heading: Owned token ranges
sections.body: Owns all key tokens falling on any of its 150 vnode positions. The set of arcs is not contiguous — that's the whole point of vnodes (spreads load + makes rebalance smooth).

sections.heading: Local write path
sections.body:
1. Append to WAL (fsync group commit)
2. Insert into memtable
3. ACK coordinator
4. Async flush memtable → L0 SST
5. Background compaction

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Disk full → writes fail fast; coordinator retries on a different replica.
- Node crash → surviving replicas still serve R reads; hinted handoff stores writes meant for this node until it returns.

gained: Excellent read latency — no compaction read amplification

bottlenecks.title: WAL fsync contention under replicated write load
bottlenecks.trigger: At 50K ops/sec cluster-wide with 1:5 write:read ratio, ~8.3K writes/sec hit the cluster. With N=3 replication, every write lands on 3 shards, so Shard A sees ~6.25K writes/sec as either primary or replica (8.3K × 3 / 4 shards). Each write requires a WAL fsync; on commodity NVMe, sustained group-commit fsync rates above ~5K/sec start queuing, and any fsync stall pins the concurrency=3000 budget since each slot waits 3-10ms on durable ack.
bottlenecks.symptom: PUT p99 latency jumps from ~10ms to >50ms, coordinator sees W=2 quorum tail dominated by A's slow ack, concurrency limiter starts rejecting with 503; on-call sees disk IO wait climbing while CPU sits idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable RocksDB group commit with batched fsync (every 1-2ms window), provision NVMe with dedicated WAL volume separate from SST volume, and set `bytes_per_sync=1MB` to smooth fsync-induced stalls. Consider `WriteOptions.sync=false` with replicated durability (W=2 across independent nodes replaces per-node fsync for many workloads).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `rocksdb.wal.fsync.latency.p99 > 15ms` for 1min, or on `rocksdb.write.stall.micros` non-zero rate. Track disk `await_ms` via node_exporter and alert >10ms sustained.

bottlenecks.title: Compaction read-amplification starves live reads during rebalance or hot-range bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: Shard A owns ~750 GB (1TB × 3 replicas / 4 shards). LSM compaction at this size, especially after a 200 GB rebalance ingest where 50M keys land in L0 at ~100 MB/s, triggers write-stall and reads must fan out across multiple SST levels. Concurrent with live 5:1 read load (~10K GETs/sec/shard), block-cache miss rate spikes and reads contend with compaction IO for the same NVMe bandwidth.
bottlenecks.symptom: GET p99 latency balloons from ~5ms to >40ms for 30-60min windows during/after rebalance; RocksDB exposes `num-running-compactions` saturated; some SST reads take 10+ms from cold cache. Coordinator sees R=2 quorum tail on reads involving A.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use leveled compaction with `max_background_compactions=4` and `level0_slowdown_writes_trigger=20`; rate-limit rebalance ingest to 50 MB/s (half the design's 100 MB/s budget) when live read QPS on shard >8K. Add a dedicated bulk-ingest SST path (RocksDB `IngestExternalFile`) to skip L0 for rebalance bytes, avoiding L0→L1 compaction churn.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `rocksdb.num-running-compactions >= max_background_compactions` sustained >5min, `rocksdb.level0.num-files > 10`, or `block_cache_hit_rate < 90%`. Track read p99 split by compaction-active vs idle periods.

bottlenecks.title: Hot vnode / hot key skew consumes disproportionate shard capacity
bottlenecks.trigger: With 150 vnodes and 4 shards (600 total), chapter reference [2] gives ~5-10% std-dev on ownership, but a single hot key (e.g., celebrity user:42 at 5K QPS) or a hot token arc can land entirely on Shard A's vnode set. At concurrency=3000 with 3-10ms service time, a single hot key consuming 5K QPS of A's budget leaves only ~70% capacity for the remaining 10K+ ops/sec of normal traffic A should handle.
bottlenecks.symptom: Shard A shows 15-20% higher CPU and QPS than B/C/D on dashboards; its p99 degrades while peers are healthy; coordinator sees A-specific ack-latency outliers skewing W=2 and R=2 quorum tails; rebalance doesn't help because the problem is key-level, not range-level.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a small in-shard LRU cache (10K entries) for hot-key GETs to shed read load without hitting RocksDB; enable per-key rate limiting at the shard with a token bucket (e.g., 1K QPS/key soft cap returning hint to coordinator for backoff); for persistent hot keys, use SDK-level key salting (key → key#shard_hint) to spread across the preference list.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit per-key QPS top-N sketch (count-min) and alert when any single key exceeds 1K QPS sustained; track per-shard QPS skew vs fleet mean and alert on >20% deviation over 5min; monitor `rocksdb.block.cache.hit` per key-prefix to spot hot-range patterns.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Shard A is here The ring and the coordinator are pure routing logic — they decide *where* a key belongs, but they don't actually hold any data. Shard A is one of the four physical machines that does the real work: storing the ~1 TB of KV pairs on disk, durably logging writes so a crash doesn't lose data, and serving reads fast enough to hit the 50K ops/sec target. Without at least one storage node per slice of the ring, the ring is just an elaborate way to point at nothing. Shard A specifically owns 150 vnode positions on the ring — a non-contiguous set of token arcs — and holds the primary or replica copy of every key that hashes into those arcs. ## What happens without it Delete Shard A and ~25% of the keyspace loses one of its three replicas. Reads for those keys now need both remaining replicas up to hit R=2 quorum, so any transient blip on B or C produces user-visible GET failures. Writes on the affected keys can still reach W=2 via the surviving replicas, but durability margin drops to zero — one more failure and data is lost. Operators see hinted-handoff buffers on B, C, D filling up with writes destined for the missing A. ## The number With RF=3 and ~1 TB of logical data, the cluster stores ~3 TB physically, spread across 4 shards — so Shard A holds roughly **750 GB**. At the rebalancer's 100 MB/s budget, re-hydrating a replacement A from peers takes ~2 hours, which is why losing a shard is survivable but not cheap. ## Trade-off Running a full LSM engine per shard gives great write throughput and compression, but you inherit compaction tuning and WAL fsync tails as operational concerns.

s2.name: Shard B (Storage Node)
s2.summary: Peer of Shard A; owns a different set of 150 vnodes on the ring.

sections.heading: Symmetry
sections.body: Shards B, C, D are identical in role to Shard A — same storage engine, same local WAL+memtable+SST pipeline, same replication behaviour. They only differ by which vnode positions they own.

sections.heading: Replica role
sections.body: For any given key, Shard B may be a primary or a replica depending on where the key hashes. There is no global primary — the ring decides per-key.

sections.heading: Hinted handoff buffer
sections.body: If a sibling is down when a write arrives, B stores a short-TTL hint locally (`hint:{down_shard}:{key}`) and replays it to the owner when the owner comes back online.

bottlenecks.title: Hinted handoff buffer growth during extended peer outage
bottlenecks.trigger: When a sibling (e.g. Shard A) is down, Shard B accepts writes on A's behalf and stores hints locally. At 8.3K cluster writes/sec × 3 replicas / 4 shards ≈ 6.25K writes/sec flowing through B, of which ~25% (~1.5K/sec) are hints for the down peer. A 1-hour outage accumulates ~5.6M hints (~5-6 GB at 1 KB/key), competing with live LSM traffic for WAL fsync, memtable space, and compaction IO on the same RocksDB instance.
bottlenecks.symptom: B's disk usage climbs steadily while A is down; WAL fsync p99 degrades from compaction churn on the hint column family; when A returns, B's replay traffic at 100+ MB/s starves live GETs and PUTs, producing a secondary latency spike 30-60min after the recovery event.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Store hints in a separate RocksDB column family with its own write-rate limit (cap at 50 MB/s replay), set a hint TTL of 3 hours (beyond which full anti-entropy/Merkle repair takes over), and reject new hints with backpressure once the hint CF exceeds 10 GB — forcing coordinators to fail writes rather than silently buffering unbounded state.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `hint_cf_size_bytes > 5 GB` or `hint_count > 1M` per shard; track `hint_replay_rate` during recovery and alert if it exceeds 50% of the shard's live-traffic IO budget; page on hint_age_p99 > 1h.

bottlenecks.title: WAL fsync saturation under triple-role write load
bottlenecks.trigger: Shard B serves as primary for its own 150 vnodes AND as replica for two neighbors' preference-list spillover. At 50K ops/sec cluster load with 1:5 write ratio (~8.3K writes/sec) and RF=3, B sees ~6.25K writes/sec. Each requires a WAL fsync; concurrency=3000 with 3-10ms service time means sustained queue depth near the limit, and any fsync latency spike past 15ms cascades into 503s.
bottlenecks.symptom: PUT p99 on keys whose preference list includes B climbs from ~10ms to >50ms; coordinator W=2 quorum tail is dominated by B's ack latency; `rocksdb.write.stall.micros` becomes non-zero; disk `await_ms` > 10ms on the WAL volume.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable group commit with 1-2ms batching window, place WAL on a dedicated NVMe volume separate from SST storage, set `bytes_per_sync=1MB` to smooth fsync stalls, and tune `max_write_buffer_number=4` so memtable flushes don't block incoming writes while compaction catches up.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `rocksdb.wal.fsync.latency.p99 > 15ms` for 1min; track `write_stall_micros_rate > 0` as a paging signal; monitor per-shard concurrency-utilization and alert when B sustains >80% of its 3000 budget.

bottlenecks.title: Non-contiguous vnode ownership amplifies compaction range-scan cost
bottlenecks.trigger: B owns ~150 non-contiguous token arcs scattered across the 2^32 ring (by design, for load spreading). RocksDB stores keys sorted by key bytes, not by token, so B's owned ranges are interleaved with keys it doesn't own only during rebalance transfers. But when a peer joins/leaves and B must stream out a subset of its 150 arcs, each arc requires a separate iterator seek, and at ~200 GB transfer at 100 MB/s the 150 seek+scan cycles plus merkle-hashing run concurrently with live compaction.
bottlenecks.symptom: During rebalance, GET p99 on B balloons from ~5ms to 30-40ms; `num-running-compactions` saturates at max_background_compactions; block cache hit rate drops below 85% because iterator scans pollute the cache with rarely-read keys; coordinator sees R=2 tails dominated by B.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use RocksDB prefix-extractor keyed on the token's high bits so each vnode arc maps to a contiguous SST key prefix, enabling `DeleteRange` + `IngestExternalFile` for bulk transfer instead of per-key iteration; cap rebalance bandwidth at 50 MB/s (half the 100 MB/s budget) when live read QPS > 8K; pin the block cache for hot-range keys via `cache_index_and_filter_blocks_with_high_priority=true`.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `rocksdb.iterator.seek.count` per minute during rebalance and alert on >10x baseline; emit rebalance_read_p99 separately from steady-state read_p99 and alert when rebalance_read_p99 > 25ms; monitor block_cache_hit_rate with a 90% floor.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Shard B is here The problem requires replication for durability — specifically N=3 copies of every key. That means for any given key, three *different* physical machines have to hold it. Shard A alone can't do that; neither can A+B. You need at least three distinct shards to satisfy N=3, and the design goes one further with four (A, B, C, D) so the cluster can lose one shard and still have three replicas for most keys. Shard B is one of those peers — architecturally identical to A, but owning a different set of 150 vnode positions on the ring. For any particular key, B might be the primary, a replica, or uninvolved entirely; the ring decides per-key, not per-shard. ## What happens without it Drop B and the cluster has three shards with N=3 replication — every key now lives on every shard, and the ring stops earning its keep. Worse, any single failure takes you to N=2, which means one more blip and writes can't reach W=2 quorum. Users see write failures during routine maintenance; operators can no longer do rolling restarts without a maintenance window; A, C, and D take 33% more load each because B's share redistributes onto them. ## The number At ~1 TB logical data with RF=3 = ~3 TB physical, four shards means B holds ~**750 GB**. Remove B and the remaining three shards each absorb ~250 GB extra — pushing them to ~1 TB each and eating into the 100 MB/s rebalance headroom. ## Trade-off You pay for a fourth machine you don't strictly need for replication, in exchange for surviving a shard loss without degrading quorum.

s3.name: Shard C (Storage Node)
s3.summary: Peer of shards A and B; owns a different set of 150 vnodes.

sections.heading: Symmetry
sections.body: Identical to Shard A in architecture; only the ring placement differs.

sections.heading: Why 3 replicas is the common choice
sections.body: With N=3, W=2, R=2: you tolerate one replica failure on both reads and writes (quorum intersection guarantees consistency when W+R>N). N=2 means any single failure blocks writes; N=4+ doubles storage cost for diminishing durability gains.

bottlenecks.title: WAL fsync saturation under combined primary + replica write load
bottlenecks.trigger: At peak 50K ops/sec with 5:1 read:write (~8.3K writes/sec) and RF=3, Shard C sees ~6.25K writes/sec across roles as primary for its 150 vnodes and replica for neighbors' preference lists. Each write requires a WAL fsync; sustained fsync rates >5K/sec on commodity NVMe start queuing, and with concurrency=3000 and 3-10ms service time, any fsync stall above 15ms pins the concurrency budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: PUT p99 latency on keys whose preference list includes C jumps from ~10ms to >50ms; coordinator W=2 quorum tails are dominated by C's ack latency; `rocksdb.write.stall.micros` becomes non-zero; on-call sees disk `await_ms` >10ms while CPU stays idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable RocksDB group commit with 1-2ms batching window, place WAL on dedicated NVMe separate from SST volume, set `bytes_per_sync=1MB` to smooth fsync stalls, and tune `max_write_buffer_number=4` so memtable flushes don't block incoming writes during compaction catch-up.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `rocksdb.wal.fsync.latency.p99 > 15ms` for 1min; page on `write_stall_micros_rate > 0`; monitor per-shard concurrency utilization and alert when C sustains >80% of its 3000 budget for >2min.

bottlenecks.title: Read quorum tail latency when C is the R=2 partner
bottlenecks.trigger: Under 5:1 read:write (~42K reads/sec cluster-wide, ~10.5K GETs/sec landing on C as either primary or R=2 partner), GET operations require R=2 acks. With ~750 GB of data per shard and LSM compaction active, any block-cache miss cascades into multi-level SST lookups at 3-10ms; a single slow C read stretches the coordinator's quorum wait since the third replica is only queried on mismatch.
bottlenecks.symptom: GET p99 balloons from ~5ms to 30-40ms during compaction windows; coordinator metrics show R=2 quorum tails skewed by C; block cache hit rate drops below 90%; users report intermittent slow reads that disappear when compaction settles.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Configure leveled compaction with `max_background_compactions=4` and `level0_slowdown_writes_trigger=20`; pin index/filter blocks via `cache_index_and_filter_blocks_with_high_priority=true`; enable speculative execution at the coordinator so a slow C response triggers a hedged read to A after p95 latency (~8ms) instead of waiting for timeout.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `get_p99_by_shard` split by compaction-active vs idle; alert when C's read p99 exceeds fleet median by >2x over 5min; track `rocksdb.block.cache.hit.rate` with 90% floor; alert on `num-running-compactions` saturated >5min.

bottlenecks.title: Quorum collapse risk from correlated C+one-peer failure
bottlenecks.trigger: With N=3, W=2, R=2, the cluster tolerates exactly one replica failure per key. For ~25% of keys whose preference list includes C plus any specific peer (say C+A), losing both simultaneously blocks writes (can't reach W=2) and blocks reads (can't reach R=2). At 4 shards this is a narrow safety margin — one planned maintenance on a sibling while C has a transient fsync stall = quorum failure for that key subset.
bottlenecks.symptom: During rolling restarts or a peer outage concurrent with C experiencing WAL stalls, coordinator returns 503 on writes for ~25% of keys; read-after-write failures spike; hinted-handoff buffers on D balloon with writes destined for C or its paired peer.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Stagger maintenance windows so no two shards in the same preference-list pair are touched within a 30min window; monitor per-shard availability and block membership changes when any shard is unhealthy; consider N=3 with sloppy quorum + hinted handoff (Dynamo-style) so writes accept a non-preference-list replica when 2 preferred replicas are down.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit `preference_list_degraded_count` metric tracking keys whose preference list has ≥1 unhealthy shard; alert when >10% of keyspace is degraded or when any two shards simultaneously report unhealthy for >60s; track sloppy-quorum write rate as an early warning.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Shard C is here The design commits to N=3 replication for durability — every key lives on three different physical machines so one machine can die without data loss. That math only works if the cluster has at least three storage nodes. Shard C is the third leg of that minimum: without it, you can't build a preference list of 3 distinct shards for any key, and the whole "walk clockwise, pick N different owners" algorithm breaks down. The ring is architectural scaffolding, but C (alongside A, B, and D) is where the bytes actually live. ## What happens without it Drop Shard C and ~75% of keys lose one of their three replicas — any key whose preference list included C now has only two copies. The coordinator can still satisfy W=2 writes and R=2 reads by leaning on the surviving two, but there's zero margin: one more shard blip and that key's writes fail with 503, or reads can't form a quorum. Operators see hinted-handoff buffers on A, B, and D filling up with writes destined for C, and any rolling restart becomes dangerous because it guarantees a second shard is briefly unavailable. ## The number At 50K ops/sec with 5:1 read:write, C handles roughly **10.5K GETs/sec** as primary or R=2 partner across its 150 vnodes. That's about a quarter of the cluster's read load — remove C and that traffic piles onto the three survivors, pushing each from ~10.5K to ~14K GETs/sec, within striking distance of their concurrency=3000 ceiling. ## Trade-off You pay for a fourth machine's storage and ops overhead to keep quorum intact during single-shard maintenance.

s4.name: Shard D (Storage Node)
s4.summary: Fourth peer shard. Present so the cluster can lose one shard and still have N=3 replicas of most keys.

sections.heading: Cluster size vs replication factor
sections.body: Cluster size must be >= N. With 4 shards and N=3, ~25% of the keyspace has one replica on each of 3 of the 4 shards; shard-loss only degrades that 75% of keys, and we can still satisfy R=2.

sections.heading: Why not 3 shards if N=3?
sections.body: With S=N, every shard holds every key and replica placement is deterministic regardless of the ring. The ring only starts earning its keep at S > N.

bottlenecks.title: Absorbing a departed peer's load pushes D past capacity
bottlenecks.trigger: If any one of A/B/C is lost, ~75% of the keyspace that referenced the downed shard in its preference list now routes to the 3 survivors — D's steady-state ~10.5K GETs/sec and ~6.25K writes/sec climb by ~33% each (to ~14K GETs and ~8.3K writes/sec), approaching its concurrency=3000 ceiling at 3-10ms service time.
bottlenecks.symptom: D's p99 latency jumps from ~10ms to >50ms; coordinator R=2 and W=2 quorum tails are dominated by D; concurrency-limit 503s appear on the shard; hinted-handoff buffers for the downed peer grow at ~1.5K writes/sec on D.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Provision each shard to run at ≤60% of concurrency budget in steady state (leaving 33% headroom for single-shard loss); enable coordinator-side hedged reads to skip a saturated D after p95 latency; cap hinted-handoff ingest rate to 25 MB/s on survivors so replay traffic doesn't compound the overload.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when per-shard concurrency utilization sustains >70% for 2min; page on `preference_list_degraded_count` >10% of keyspace combined with any shard's p99 >30ms; track hinted-handoff buffer size on D with a 5 GB ceiling.

bottlenecks.title: Rebalance ingest from a 5th-shard join competes with live traffic
bottlenecks.trigger: When shard E joins, D streams out ~38 of the 150 new E-owned ranges (~50 GB at 100 MB/s ≈ 8-10 min of sustained outbound IO), while simultaneously serving its ~10.5K GETs/sec and ~6.25K writes/sec. RocksDB iterator scans for outbound ranges pollute the block cache and share NVMe bandwidth with live reads and WAL fsync.
bottlenecks.symptom: During the ~35min rebalance window, D's GET p99 climbs from ~5ms to 30-40ms; block cache hit rate falls below 85%; WAL fsync p99 degrades as iterator scans and SST reads saturate disk queue depth; coordinators see D-skewed quorum tails on both reads and writes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Rate-limit outbound transfer on D to 50 MB/s (half the 100 MB/s budget) when live QPS >8K; use RocksDB `IngestExternalFile` + prefix-bounded iterators so outbound scans don't evict hot blocks; pin index/filter blocks via `cache_index_and_filter_blocks_with_high_priority=true`; schedule rebalances during low-traffic windows.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit `rebalance_outbound_mb_s` and `live_read_p99` as separate metrics; alert when rebalance-active p99 exceeds 25ms or when block_cache_hit_rate drops below 90% during transfer; track disk `await_ms` with a 10ms ceiling.

bottlenecks.title: WAL fsync saturation under combined primary + replica write load
bottlenecks.trigger: At 50K ops/sec cluster-wide with 1:5 write ratio (~8.3K writes/sec) and RF=3, D sees ~6.25K writes/sec across its primary role for 150 vnodes and replica role for neighbors. Each write requires a WAL fsync; sustained rates >5K/sec on commodity NVMe start queuing, and any fsync stall above 15ms pins the concurrency=3000 budget at 3-10ms service time.
bottlenecks.symptom: PUT p99 on keys whose preference list includes D climbs from ~10ms to >50ms; `rocksdb.write.stall.micros` becomes non-zero; coordinator W=2 tails are skewed by D; disk `await_ms` >10ms on the WAL volume while CPU stays idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable RocksDB group commit with 1-2ms batching window; place WAL on dedicated NVMe separate from SST volume; set `bytes_per_sync=1MB` to smooth fsync stalls; tune `max_write_buffer_number=4` so memtable flushes don't block incoming writes during compaction catch-up.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `rocksdb.wal.fsync.latency.p99 >15ms` for 1min; page on `write_stall_micros_rate >0`; monitor D's concurrency utilization with an 80% alert threshold over 2min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Shard D is here The design commits to N=3 replication — every key lives on three different machines so one can die without data loss. That means the cluster must have *at least* three storage nodes. But if you run exactly three (A, B, C), every key lives on every shard, and the ring stops doing anything useful — there's no placement choice to make. Worse, the moment any shard goes down for a routine reboot, you're at N=2 with zero safety margin: one more blip and writes can't form a W=2 quorum. Shard D is the fourth leg that gives the cluster headroom above the replication minimum, so ops work like rolling restarts and OS patching stop being white-knuckle events. ## What happens without it Remove D and take A down for maintenance. Now ~100% of the keyspace is at N=2. A GC pause on B lasting 500ms means coordinators can't reach W=2 for any write hashing to A-B-C's preference list — the user sees write failures, the operator sees a 503 spike, and C absorbs emergency read load from every key that normally would have fanned out to 3 replicas. ## The number The design holds ~1 TB logical × RF=3 = **~3 TB physical**, split across 4 shards at ~750 GB each. Drop to 3 shards and each holds ~1 TB — and losing one during rebalance at 100 MB/s means ~2.8 hours of degraded quorum instead of a brief blip. ## Trade-off You pay for a fourth machine you don't strictly need for replication, to keep maintenance routine instead of risky.

rebal.name: Background Rebalancer
rebal.summary: Long-running job that moves keys between shards when the ring topology changes (join, leave, weight change).

sections.heading: Trigger
sections.body: Membership gossip says a new shard joined or an existing one was removed. The rebalancer computes the delta between the old and new ring and enumerates key ranges that now have a different owner.

sections.heading: Algorithm (minimal-movement)
sections.body:
1. Diff old ring vs new ring → list of `(token_range, old_owner, new_owner)` transfers
2. For each range, stream keys from old_owner → new_owner using a bounded-bandwidth channel
3. Once new_owner acks, update the authoritative membership record and let gossip propagate
4. Old owner tombstones (or TTLs) the transferred range locally

sections.heading: Backpressure
sections.body: Throttle per-shard transfer to ~100 MB/s to protect live traffic. At 200 GB to move, a full rebalance runs in ~35 min per new shard.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Rebalancer crash mid-transfer: keys are now on BOTH old and new owner. Reads still work (same data); writes go to new owner by the new ring. A resumable checkpoint avoids restarting the whole range.
- Network partition during transfer: pause and resume when healed — the source retains the range until acked.

lost: Cluster is read-only (or offline) during the rebalance

bottlenecks.title: Throttled transfer bandwidth extends vulnerability window during rebalance
bottlenecks.trigger: On a 5th-shard join, the rebalancer must move ~200 GB (1/5 of the 1 TB dataset) at the 100 MB/s per-shard cap, taking ~35 min; on a shard loss requiring re-replication of ~750 GB across survivors, the window stretches to ~2 hours. During this window, any second failure degrades quorum (N=3 → N=2) for the affected ranges.
bottlenecks.symptom: Prolonged periods where some keys have only 2 live replicas, elevated risk of W=2 failures if another shard blips, and coordinators seeing hinted-handoff buffers swell on surviving shards; on-call sees rebalance progress dashboards crawling while SLO error budgets burn.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Dynamic bandwidth scaling: start at 50 MB/s and ramp to 200 MB/s based on live-traffic headroom (p99 latency < 20ms on source shard); prioritize transfer of under-replicated ranges (N=2) over simple topology rebalances; use RocksDB `IngestExternalFile` for bulk SST injection to skip L0 compaction on the destination.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `rebalance_eta_seconds` and alert when projected completion >1h; emit `under_replicated_key_count` with a page threshold at >1% of keyspace sustained >10min; monitor `rebalance_bandwidth_utilization` vs configured cap.

bottlenecks.title: Mid-transfer crash leaves keys double-owned with ambiguous write routing
bottlenecks.trigger: Rebalancer failure rate is 0.002 across 35+ min transfers with 217 ranges per join. A crash mid-range means keys exist on BOTH old_owner and new_owner, and the ring commit (version bump) may or may not have propagated to all coordinators. Concurrent with ring_version=17 coordinators writing to old_owner and ring_version=18 coordinators writing to new_owner, read-after-write sees divergent values.
bottlenecks.symptom: After rebalancer restart, intermittent stale reads (GET returns pre-transfer value from old_owner while PUT landed on new_owner), conflict-resolution metrics spike at storage nodes, duplicate storage cost during the overlap window, and operators see ambiguous `tombstone_pending` state with unclear cleanup ownership.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Persist per-range transfer checkpoints to a durable metadata store (etcd/Raft) with states {PLANNED, STREAMING, VERIFIED, COMMITTED, TOMBSTONED}; never commit the ring version bump until ALL ranges reach VERIFIED; on restart, resume from checkpoint and re-verify Merkle roots rather than restart ranges; require coordinators to tag RPCs with ring_version so storage nodes can return NotOwner+hint for stale-version writes during the overlap.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit `rebalance_ranges_in_flight` and `rebalance_ranges_stuck` (STREAMING state >10min without progress); alert on `ring_version_skew` across coordinator fleet >30s; track `dual_owned_range_count` from gossip and page when non-zero outside active transfer windows.

bottlenecks.title: Parallel source streams saturate destination shard's LSM ingest
bottlenecks.trigger: When shard E joins, all 4 existing shards (A/B/C/D) stream ~50 GB each concurrently to E at 100 MB/s per source = aggregate ~400 MB/s inbound to E. E's RocksDB must absorb this into L0 while simultaneously serving new live traffic for the ~1/5 keyspace it now owns at ~10K ops/sec, triggering write stalls and L0→L1 compaction backpressure.
bottlenecks.symptom: E's inbound transfer rate fluctuates wildly as RocksDB write stalls kick in, extending the 35min rebalance to 60+ min; GETs on newly-transferred keys see 30-40ms p99 during the ingest window; `rocksdb.level0.num-files` saturates and compaction debt grows visibly on E; coordinator sees E-skewed latency immediately after ring v18 commit.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Coordinate source streams through the rebalancer to cap aggregate destination ingest at 150 MB/s regardless of source count; use RocksDB `IngestExternalFile` with pre-sorted SSTs so transferred data lands directly at L1+ bypassing memtable and L0; delay ring commit on E until L0 file count drops below 10, ensuring steady-state read latency before exposing E to live traffic.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `destination_ingest_mb_s` and alert when >200 MB/s sustained >1min; monitor E's `rocksdb.num-level0-files` with threshold >15; emit `rebalance_destination_write_stall_micros` and alert on non-zero rate during active transfer.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Rebalancer is here The ring tells you *where* a key should live, but it doesn't actually move bytes. When shard E joins and the ring is updated to include E's 150 new vnodes, ~200 GB of keys that used to live on A, B, C, D now belong to E — but they're still physically sitting on the old shards. Until someone copies that data across the network, E owns ranges it has no data for, and reads to those keys would miss. The Background Rebalancer is the worker that walks the diff between the old and new ring, streams the affected keys to their new home, and then flips the authoritative ring version once E has verified it has everything. ## What happens without it Without a rebalancer, adding a shard is a paper change: the ring says E owns 1/5 of the keyspace, but E's disk is empty. Users issuing GETs for keys that hash to E get "not found" for data that definitely exists on A. Operators see a cluster that looks healthy in membership gossip but is silently serving wrong answers. The storage shards take the hit indirectly — coordinators start fanning out to all replicas hunting for the missing data, amplifying read load 3×. ## The number The capacity plan says adding a 5th shard moves **~200 GB** at a throttled **100 MB/s per shard**, giving ~35 min to drain. Run that unthrottled and live traffic collapses; skip the throttle entirely and the 5:1 read:write mix at 50K ops/sec loses its IO budget to backfill. ## Trade-off You accept a ~35-minute window where keys briefly exist on *both* old and new owners, in exchange for zero-downtime topology changes.

operations.title: PUT key (hash → route → replicate to N, wait for W acks)
operations.name: PUT key (hash → route → replicate to N, wait for W acks)
operations.description: Client writes `user:42 → {...}`. Coordinator hashes the key, looks up the N=3 preference list on the ring, writes to all 3 in parallel, and acks the client once W=2 replicas have committed.

steps.title: Client issues PUT
steps.action: The client SDK sends a PUT to any coordinator with the key, value, and an idempotency id.

steps.title: Coordinator receives PUT and hashes the key
steps.action: The coordinator MurmurHashes the key to a 32-bit token and looks up the preference list on its cached ring view.
steps.codeOrCommand:
token = murmur3_32("user:42") # e.g. 0x7F2A_9B44
pref_list = ring.preference_list(token, N=3)
# → [Shard B (primary), Shard C (replica), Shard A (replica)]

steps.title: Ring returns preference list of N distinct shards
steps.action: Binary search on the sorted (token → vnode → shard) array, then walk clockwise collecting distinct physical shards until N=3 are found.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# sorted ring of 600 (token, shard) tuples
idx = upper_bound(ring.tokens, 0x7F2A9B44)
owners = for i in range(len(ring)): s = ring.shard_at((idx + i) % len(ring)) if s not in owners: owners.append(s) if len(owners) == 3: break
return owners # [B, C, A]
steps.note: Distinct-owner filter is critical — without it, replicas could all land on the same physical shard via adjacent vnodes.

steps.title: Shard B (primary for this key) commits write
steps.action: Shard B receives the PUT, appends to WAL, inserts into the memtable, and acks. Coordinator dispatches to C and A in parallel.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# RocksDB
wal.append(WriteBatch.Put("user:42", value))
wal.sync # group fsync
memtable.put("user:42", value)
return OK

steps.title: Shard C commits replica write (parallel)
steps.action: Same local write path as shard B, running concurrently. The second ack satisfies W=2.
steps.codeOrCommand:
wal.append(WriteBatch.Put("user:42", value))
wal.sync
memtable.put("user:42", value)
return OK

steps.title: Shard A commits replica write (parallel, but not needed for W=2)
steps.action: Shard A's ack arrives after the coordinator has already replied to the client. Still recorded for durability.
steps.codeOrCommand:
wal.append(WriteBatch.Put("user:42", value))
wal.sync
memtable.put("user:42", value)
return OK

steps.title: Coordinator aggregates acks; W=2 reached
steps.action: Once 2 of 3 replicas ack, coordinator returns success to the client. The 3rd ack (from A) continues asynchronously.
steps.codeOrCommand:
acks = 0
for resp in as_completed(futures, timeout=100ms): if resp.ok: acks += 1 if acks >= W: # W = 2 return 200
steps.decision: W quorum satisfied with B+C. A finishes asynchronously.

steps.title: Client receives OK
steps.action: Total latency ≈ hash + ring lookup + max(WAL fsync on the 2nd-fastest replica) + network. Typically 8–20ms.

operations.title: GET key (hash → route → read from nearest replica)
operations.name: GET key (hash → route → read from nearest replica)
operations.description: Client reads `user:42`. Coordinator hashes, picks N shards from the ring, and requests from the nearest (lowest-latency) replica first; falls back to others for R=2 quorum.

steps.title: Client issues GET
steps.action: Client requests key `user:42`.

steps.title: Coordinator hashes key and consults ring
steps.action: Same hash + ring lookup as on write. Preference list [B, C, A] is produced in sub-microsecond time.
steps.codeOrCommand:
token = murmur3_32("user:42")
pref_list = ring.preference_list(token, N=3) # [B, C, A]
nearest = health.pick_fastest(pref_list) # e.g. B

steps.title: Ring returns same preference list [B, C, A]
steps.action: Consistent hashing guarantees the same ordered list for a given key as long as the ring topology is unchanged — reads and writes see the same replicas.

steps.title: Shard B reads from memtable or SST
steps.action: Local RocksDB Get. May hit memtable (most recently written) or fall through to block cache / SSTs.

steps.title: Shard C reads in parallel (for R=2 quorum)
steps.action: Coordinator also reads from C to satisfy R=2. If B and C return the same version, consistency is confirmed without touching A.

steps.title: Coordinator checks R=2 and returns
steps.action: Two responses with matching versions → consistent read. Return the value to the client. Shard A is not queried.
steps.codeOrCommand:
responses = [B_resp, C_resp]
if all(r.version == responses[0].version for r in responses): return responses[0].value
else: # conflict: either wait for A or resolve via vector clock...
steps.decision: R=2 satisfied, versions agree — no conflict resolution needed.

steps.title: Client receives value
steps.action: Total latency typically 5–12ms. Read quorum keeps stale data from slipping through even if one replica is lagging.

operations.title: Node added: minimal-movement rebalance
operations.name: Node added: minimal-movement rebalance
operations.description: A fifth shard E joins the cluster. The ring adds 150 new vnodes for E. The rebalancer computes which token ranges now belong to E and streams only those keys — roughly 1/5 of the total keyspace, not 100%.

steps.title: Rebalancer detects new shard E via gossip
steps.action: The rebalancer observes a membership event: `shard E joined, 150 vnodes assigned`. It diffs the pre-join ring (600 vnodes, 4 owners) vs the post-join ring (750 vnodes, 5 owners).
steps.codeOrCommand:
diff = ring_diff(old_ring, new_ring)
# → list of (token_range, old_owner, new_owner='E')
# e.g. 217 small arcs totalling ~200 GB of key space
print(f"ranges to transfer: {len(diff)}, est bytes: {sum(r.size for r in diff)}")

steps.title: Ring computes minimal-movement delta
steps.action: For each of E's 150 new vnode tokens, walk backwards to the previous vnode and the arc between them is the range E now owns. The previous vnode's owner is the source for that range.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Pseudocode for delta computation
ranges = for token in E.vnode_tokens: prev = old_ring.predecessor(token) source = old_ring.shard_at(prev) ranges.append((prev + 1, token, source, 'E'))
return ranges # 150 transfer ranges

steps.title: Shard A streams its transferring ranges to E
steps.action: Some of E's new vnodes sit just clockwise of A's vnodes — those arcs move from A to E. A opens a streaming RocksDB iterator scoped to the outgoing token ranges.
steps.codeOrCommand:
for (start, end) in ranges_from_A: it = rocksdb.new_iterator it.seek(start) while it.valid and hash(it.key) <= end: stream.send(it.key, it.value) it.next
stream.flush

steps.title: Shard B streams its share (parallel)
steps.action: Same behaviour as A, but for B's slice of the transfer plan. Each old owner streams in parallel at throttled ~100 MB/s.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# same iterator pattern, bounded bandwidth
for (start, end) in ranges_from_B: stream_range(start, end, dest="E", rate_limit_mb_s=100)

steps.title: Shard C streams its share (parallel)
steps.action: C's portion of the transfer plan. Reads here proceed as normal — the outgoing range is still served from C until the transfer commits.

steps.title: Shard D streams its share (parallel)
steps.action: D's portion. After all four sources drain, E owns its full ~1/5 slice and the old owners can tombstone the transferred ranges.

steps.title: Rebalancer commits the ring change
steps.action: Once E acks all ranges and verifies a Merkle root against each source, the rebalancer publishes the new ring version. Gossip propagates version 18 to coordinators within seconds.
steps.decision: Minimal-movement invariant held: ~1/5 of keys moved, rest stayed put.
steps.note: Modulo hashing would have moved ~100% of keys for the same cluster-size change — a 5x cost. This is the whole reason consistent hashing exists.

tradeoffs.decision: Number of virtual nodes per physical shard
tradeoffs.rationale: Below 100 the load std-dev exceeds 15%; above 500 the gossip/ring state grows without noticeably better balance.

tradeoffs.decision: Hash function: SHA-1 vs MurmurHash3 vs xxHash
tradeoffs.rationale: Cryptographic strength is irrelevant for routing, and a faster hash shrinks lookup latency to sub-microsecond.
Modulo-N moves ~(N-1)/N of all keys when N changes, causing a cache-miss storm; consistent hashing moves only 1/N.

tradeoffs.decision: Ring stored centrally vs embedded in smart clients
tradeoffs.rationale: Embedding skips a network hop per request at the cost of shipping ring updates via gossip — worthwhile above 10K QPS per client.

tradeoffs.decision: Virtual nodes vs bounded-load consistent hashing
tradeoffs.rationale: Bounded-load (Google's 2017 paper) gives tighter guarantees but requires per-node counters and extra coordination — overkill for most use cases.

tradeoffs.decision: Copy-on-write ring vs read-write lock on mutation
tradeoffs.rationale: Node joins are rare (minutes apart); a ReadWriteLock gives concurrent lookups without paying the GC cost of copying the TreeMap on every change.
